source.title_on_document: The role of task breadth and cognitive flexibility in generative AI-supported creative idea generation

supplement.where: Appendices A-E are included in the article PDF (pp. 13-19); no separate online supplement is mentioned.
supplement.holds: Appendix D (p. 18) contains arm-specific expert novelty, usefulness and creativity ratings and idea-count means, SDs and Ns, without inferential tests; its interpretation (p. 19) also states that AI-exposed participants produced shorter ideas on average, without a named study, measurement procedure or statistics. Appendix E (p. 19) contains Shapiro-Wilk normality tests and density plots. Appendices A-C (pp. 13-18) contain the generator prompt, arm instructions and semantic-category coding scheme.

paper_design_summary: Two online between-subjects experiments on startup idea generation, run before ChatGPT's release. Participants were randomly assigned to see a static list of ideas from a GPT-3 startup-idea generator that the paper calls fine-tuned (10 ideas in Study 1, a broad task, 90 master's students analyzed; 4 education ideas in Study 2, a narrow EdTech task, 117 UK Prolific entrepreneurs analyzed) or no AI ideas, and then wrote their own startup ideas for about 10 minutes. Scored outcomes are breadth of exploration (hand-coded semantic categories per participant), depth (ideas per category), embedding similarity among participants' ideas within each arm, and, in Appendix D, expert novelty, usefulness and creativity ratings and the number of ideas.

studies.label: Study 1 (broad startup idea task, master's students)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Exposure to 10 randomly drawn ideas from a GPT-3 startup-idea generator (called fine-tuned by the paper) versus no AI-generated ideas
assignment.quote: Ninety-three participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: exposed to ideas generated by a fine-tuned LLM (n = 46) or no exposure to LLM-generated ideas (n = 47).
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration mentioned anywhere in the paper; an a priori G*Power analysis is reported (p. 6, Section 4.1)

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Shown 10 ideas randomly drawn from a database of 453 GPT-3 startup ideas, told they were generated by artificial intelligence, free to use them as inspiration but not to suggest an identical idea; told they could do some internet research (Appendix B, p. 14)

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same scenario, instructions and Qualtrics interface with no AI-generated ideas; told they could do some internet research, as in the AI arm (same interface: p. 7, Section 4.2; instructions: Appendix B, p. 14)

participants.exclusions: Three participants were excluded because they failed to complete the experiment (p. 6, Section 4.1). The paper does not report exclusions separately by arm. It reports 46 and 47 randomized (p. 6, Section 4.1) and 45 and 45 analyzed (p. 8, Section 4.6; Table 4, p. 9). The analysis excludes non-completers and is not intention-to-treat; no unreported per-arm exclusion counts are recorded.
participants.who: International master's students specializing in management who had attended at least one entrepreneurship course; average age about 23; 65% female; 91% took the study in French, 9% in English. Recruited by cold electronic messaging; the study ran online at participants' convenience.
participants.quote: Three participants were excluded from the final analysis because they failed to complete the experiment, leaving 90 participants.

ai_tool.name_model: 'Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI' (ideasai.net, 2022), a GPT-3 startup-idea generator the paper calls fine-tuned; Appendix A shows a prompt listing ideas labeled 'Good idea:' or 'Bad idea:' from online users' votes. 488 ideas generated; 453 kept after removing incoherent ideas and ideas describing existing companies (p. 7, Section 4.2).
ai_tool.how_used: A static list of 10 pre-generated ideas displayed on the idea-submission page as optional inspiration; participants did not interact with the model. The study ran before ChatGPT's release (p. 6, Section 4.2; Appendix B, p. 14).

task.description: Suggest startup ideas likely to be funded by an incubator (business need, product or service, major source of revenue, target customer); any domain allowed (broad task)
task.duration: Minimum 8 min, instructed to spend about 10 min, no maximum (p. 8, Section 4.5)

outcomes.name: Breadth of exploration (number of semantic categories spanned by a participant's ideas)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct semantic categories (15, derived inductively) spanned by a participant's ideas. One author built the coding scheme; an independent external researcher confirmed it and assigned each idea to a category; agreement 99 percent within 1 point, ICC 0.97; scores averaged across the two raters (p. 7, Section 4.4.1; Appendix C). The hypothesized outcome. Kruskal-Wallis test; parametric tests said to give similar conclusions (p. 8, Section 4.6.1); results unchanged when participants who failed the manipulation check are dropped (p. 7, Section 4.3).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human M = 2.32 (SD 1.32, N 45) vs human-only M = 1.60 (SD 0.74, N 45); d = 0.67. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 6.43, p = 0.01; remains significant after a Holm-Bonferroni correction for the two primary outcome tests.

outcomes.name: Depth of exploration (number of ideas divided by breadth)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas divided by breadth of exploration (ideas per explored category), read as a consequence of cognitive persistence. No hypothesis was stated for it (p. 8, Section 4.4.2), but the paper tests it as one of 'the two primary outcome tests' under a Holm-Bonferroni correction (p. 8, Section 4.6.1). Kruskal-Wallis test. Parametric tests are reported to yield similar conclusions for both breadth and depth (p. 8, Section 4.6.1).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human M = 1.13 (SD 0.26, N 45) vs human-only M = 1.15 (SD 0.33, N 45); d = 0.07 as printed (positive, although the AI-arm mean is lower). Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.45, p = 0.50.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity among participants' first ideas within each condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Only each participant's first idea kept. Preprocessing: tokenization, stop-word removal, removal of common words (e.g. startup, need, idea, revenue, customer), lemmatization, punctuation removal; SpaCy sentence embeddings; average pairwise cosine similarity within each condition. Higher value = more similar, so the sign is reversed for diversity. Described as a complementary, exploratory group-level analysis, not a hypothesis test (p. 8, Section 4.6.2).

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity (higher = more alike; sign reversed for diversity): human-only M = 0.81 (SD 0.08, N ideas 45) vs LLM-assisted human M = 0.74 (SD 0.13, N ideas 45); M difference = 0.07, 95% CI [0.04, 0.10], p = 0.00, Cohen's d = 0.91 (permutation test, 10,000 iterations). No SE printed. The AI arm's ideas are less similar, i.e. more diverse.

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings within a condition
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SpaCy package sentence embeddings (model not named)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of first ideas (one per participant) within each condition
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 10,000 iterations comparing average within-group similarity; 95% CI, permutation p-value and Cohen's d reported
diversity_detail.notes: The paper reports similarity, so the diversity sign is reversed. The paper does not say what the SDs are computed over (pairs or ideas); Table 7 gives N in ideas (45 per condition). No SE printed.

outcomes.name: Average creativity (mean of novelty and usefulness), expert rated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique: each idea rated by at least two of six expert judges (entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship program heads, an accelerator jury member, a consultant, a serial entrepreneur) on 7-point scales; creativity = mean of novelty and usefulness; idea scores averaged within participant; agreement within 1.5 points 84.6 percent. Descriptive and exploratory only (Appendix D, p. 18).

contrasts.reported: M (SD, N): LLM-assisted human 4.23 (0.37, 45) vs human-only 4.35 (0.44, 45). No test reported; direction is the sign of the printed means only.

outcomes.name: Average novelty, expert rated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three items (newness, uniqueness, unusualness), 7-point scales, at least two expert judges per idea, idea scores averaged within participant; agreement within 1.5 points 68.4 percent (Appendix D, p. 18).

contrasts.reported: M (SD, N): LLM-assisted human 3.90 (0.79, 45) vs human-only 3.97 (0.72, 45). No test reported; direction is the sign of the printed means only.

outcomes.name: Average usefulness, expert rated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Feasibility and operability items on 7-point scales; a third usefulness item, which judges read as viability, was dropped after Study 1 for low internal consistency, and the paper does not say whether the Study 1 score includes it. At least two expert judges per idea; agreement within 1.5 points 65.5 percent; idea scores averaged within participant (Appendix D, p. 18).

contrasts.reported: M (SD, N): LLM-assisted human 4.57 (0.54, 45) vs human-only 4.73 (0.69, 45). No test reported; direction is the sign of the printed means only.

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of all ideas a participant generated; 208 ideas in total, 2.3 per participant (p. 8, Section 4.6; Appendix D, p. 18).

contrasts.reported: M (SD, N): LLM-assisted human 2.71 (1.90, 45) vs human-only 1.91 (1.40, 45). No test reported; direction is the sign of the printed means only.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity: human-only ideas vs the pool of LLM-generated stimulus ideas
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Compares within-group similarity of the human-only condition's ideas with the pool of LLM-generated stimulus ideas, using the same SpaCy cosine-similarity procedure. AI output versus human output; no person receives AI help in either group (p. 8, Section 4.6.2).

contrasts.reported: M difference = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.12, -0.09], p = 0.00, Cohen's d = -1.74 (similarity; the LLM pool is less similar, i.e. more diverse). The pool's similarity level for this comparison is not printed. Separately, removing incoherent ideas moved the pool's average pairwise cosine similarity from 0.68 to 0.69 (p. 7, Section 4.2).

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SpaCy package sentence embeddings (model not named)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs within the human-only condition's ideas versus pairs within the pool of LLM-generated stimulus ideas
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Called 'a parallel comparison' right after the 10,000-iteration permutation test; the method is not restated. 95% CI, p and Cohen's d reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Context only (AI output versus human output). No SE printed.

studies.label: Study 2 (narrow EdTech startup idea task, Prolific UK entrepreneurs)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Exposure to 4 randomly drawn education-related ideas from the same GPT-3 startup-idea generator versus no AI-generated ideas
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: use of LLM-generated ideas (n = 60) versus no use (n = 60).
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration mentioned; the same power considerations as Study 1 (p. 9, Section 5.1)

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Shown 4 ideas randomly drawn (different for each participant) from 44 education-related ideas from the same generator, labeled as suggestions from an AI system, free to ignore them (p. 9, Sections 5.2-5.3; Appendix B, p. 14)

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same EdTech scenario and instructions with no AI-generated suggestions (Appendix B, p. 14)

participants.exclusions: Five ideas and three participants were excluded for unrelatedness to the task; re-including these observations leaves breadth and depth results qualitatively unchanged (p. 9, Section 5.1). The paper does not report exclusions separately by arm. It reports 60 and 60 randomized (p. 9, Section 5.1) and 59 and 58 analyzed (p. 9, Section 5.5; Table 6, p. 11). The coding scheme still lists an out-of-instruction-scope category with five ideas (p. 9, Section 5.4; Appendix C, p. 16), so whether that category enters the reported breadth scores remains unclear. The main analysis excludes participants and is not intention-to-treat.
participants.who: Prolific Academic UK panel members pre-screened on prior approval rate and English proficiency; all self-declared current engagement in entrepreneurship or owning a business; average age about 43; more than 90% born in the UK; 51% female
participants.quote: Five ideas and three participants were excluded from the final analysis because of unrelatedness to the task at hand

ai_tool.name_model: Same GPT-3 startup-idea generator as Study 1 ('Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI'); 44 education-related ideas selected (p. 9, Section 5.2)
ai_tool.how_used: A static list of 4 pre-generated ideas displayed on the idea-submission page as optional inspiration; no interaction with the model. The study ran before the public release of generative AI models (p. 9, Sections 5.2-5.3; Appendix B, p. 14).

task.description: Propose startup ideas on technology in education (need, target customer, technological solution, expected source of revenue); narrow task
task.duration: Minimum 8 min, instructed to spend about 10 min; whole participation about 11 min (p. 9, Section 5.4)

outcomes.name: Breadth of exploration (number of semantic categories spanned by a participant's ideas)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct semantic categories (11, one of them 'out of instruction scope (with five ideas)') spanned by a participant's ideas; one author coded all ideas and an external researcher reviewed the scheme and the coding (p. 9, Section 5.4; Appendix C). The hypothesized outcome. Kruskal-Wallis test; a parametric test said to give the same conclusions (p. 10, Section 5.5.1); results unchanged when participants who failed the manipulation check are dropped (p. 9, Section 5.3). A posteriori reanalysis re-including the five excluded ideas and three excluded participants leaves breadth and depth results qualitatively unchanged (p. 9, Section 5.1). Whether the out-of-instruction-scope category enters the reported main-analysis breadth scores is not stated.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human M = 1.39 (SD 0.70, N 59) vs human-only M = 1.38 (SD 0.67, N 58); d = 0.01. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.00, p = 1.00.

outcomes.name: Depth of exploration (number of ideas divided by breadth)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideas per explored semantic category, read as a consequence of cognitive persistence; not hypothesized, but named with breadth as one of the paper's 'primary theory-driven analyses' (p. 10, Section 5.5.1). Kruskal-Wallis test. A parametric test yields the same conclusions for both breadth and depth (p. 10, Section 5.5.1). A posteriori reanalysis re-including the five excluded ideas and three excluded participants leaves both results qualitatively unchanged (p. 9, Section 5.1).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human M = 1.16 (SD 0.48, N 59) vs human-only M = 1.11 (SD 0.35, N 58); d = 0.12. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.07, p = 0.79.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity among participants' ideas within each condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Analyses 'parallel to those in Study 1' (SpaCy sentence embeddings, average pairwise cosine similarity within condition, permutation test with 10,000 iterations); the first-idea rule is implied by 'parallel', and Table 7 lists 59 and 58 ideas. Higher value = more similar. Described as exploratory (p. 10, Section 5.5.2).

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity (higher = more alike; sign reversed for diversity): human-only M = 0.87 (SD 0.04, N ideas 58) vs LLM-assisted human M = 0.87 (SD 0.05, N ideas 59); M difference = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.02], p = 0.09, Cohen's d = 0.31 (permutation test, 10,000 iterations). No SE printed; the sign convention of the 0.01 difference is not stated.

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings within a condition
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SpaCy package sentence embeddings (model not named)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs of ideas within each condition; the text calls the analysis parallel to Study 1 (first idea per participant), and Table 7 lists 59 and 58 ideas
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 10,000 iterations; 95% CI, permutation p-value and Cohen's d reported
diversity_detail.notes: The paper reports similarity, so the diversity sign is reversed. Both arm means print as 0.87 and the direction of the 0.01 difference is not stated. What the SDs are computed over is not stated. No SE printed.

outcomes.name: Average creativity (mean of novelty and usefulness), expert rated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two expert judges rated all 183 ideas on 7-point scales; initial agreement on usefulness was insufficient, so the judges discussed discrepancies before final aggregation; creativity = mean of novelty and usefulness; idea scores averaged within participant. Descriptive and exploratory only (Appendix D, p. 18).

contrasts.reported: M (SD, N): LLM-assisted human 4.86 (0.74, 59) vs human-only 4.52 (0.88, 58). No test reported; direction is the sign of the printed means only.

outcomes.name: Average novelty, expert rated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three items (newness, uniqueness, unusualness), 7-point scales, two expert judges, idea scores averaged within participant (Appendix D, p. 18).

contrasts.reported: M (SD, N): LLM-assisted human 4.61 (0.87, 59) vs human-only 4.41 (0.91, 58). No test reported; direction is the sign of the printed means only.

outcomes.name: Average usefulness, expert rated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Feasibility and operability items (the third item was dropped after Study 1), 7-point scales, two expert judges who discussed discrepancies before final aggregation, idea scores averaged within participant (Appendix D, p. 18).

contrasts.reported: M (SD, N): LLM-assisted human 5.11 (1.04, 59) vs human-only 4.60 (1.16, 58). No test reported; direction is the sign of the printed means only.

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of all ideas a participant generated; 183 ideas in total, 1.56 per participant (p. 9, Section 5.5; Appendix D, p. 18).

contrasts.reported: M (SD, N): LLM-assisted human 1.61 (1.02, 59) vs human-only 1.52 (0.78, 58). No test reported; direction is the sign of the printed means only.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity: human-only ideas vs the pool of LLM-generated education stimulus ideas
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise cosine similarity of the education-related LLM stimulus pool, reported descriptively beside the participant conditions. This context record retains only the comparison with the human-only arm, which received no AI suggestions; the assisted arm is not an unassisted human comparator. The paper notes that the pool contains education ideas more broadly, rather than direct outputs of the EdTech experimental task (p. 10, Section 5.5.2; p. 11, Table 7).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Pool of LLM-generated education ideas used as stimuli
contrasts.reported: LLM stimulus pool M = 0.77 (SD = 0.10) vs human-only ideas M = 0.87 (SD = 0.04, N ideas = 58; Table 7). No test, SE, interval or standardized effect is reported for this pool comparison; the direction indicates lower similarity, hence greater diversity, in the stimulus pool. The pool N is not printed with its statistic; the stimulus database held 44 ideas (p. 9, Section 5.2).
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 5.2 (stimulus database); p. 10, Section 5.5.2; p. 11, Table 7

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SpaCy package sentence embeddings (model not named)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs within the LLM-generated education stimulus pool, compared descriptively with pairs within the human-only arm; the assisted participant arm is excluded from this context contrast.
diversity_detail.notes: Context only: AI-generated output versus unassisted human output. The paper discusses both participant conditions, but this record restricts the comparator to the human-only arm to meet the codebook definition. Stimuli cover education more broadly than the EdTech task; no causal inference about stimulus source follows from this descriptive comparison.

eligibility.reason: Both studies independently meet all three criteria. Individuals were randomly assigned to GPT-3-generated idea suggestions or no AI suggestions (p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 9, Section 5.1), available while participants produced their own startup ideas (p. 14, Appendix B). Study 1 analyzed 90 people, 45 per arm (p. 8, Section 4.6; p. 9, Table 4); Study 2 analyzed 117 people, 59 and 58 per arm (p. 9, Section 5.5; p. 11, Table 6). These are counts after exclusions, not counts of ideas or ratings. Hand-coded breadth, across-participant semantic similarity, and expert novelty, usefulness and creativity ratings are scored on the produced ideas (pp. 7-10, Sections 4.4.1, 4.6.2, 5.4 and 5.5.2; p. 18, Appendix D). Unspecified idea-length methods and possible overlap with earlier publications affect extraction or deduplication, not these eligibility findings.

one_line_finding: Seeing GPT-3-generated startup ideas raised breadth of exploration in the broad Study 1 task (2.32 vs 1.60 categories, d = 0.67, Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.01; p. 8, Section 4.6.1; Table 4, p. 9) and lowered similarity among participants' first ideas (0.74 vs 0.81, permutation p = 0.00; Table 7, p. 11), but showed no statistically significant difference in either in the narrow Study 2 EdTech task (breadth 1.39 vs 1.38, p = 1.00, p. 10, Section 5.5.1; Table 6; similarity 0.87 vs 0.87, p = 0.09, Table 7; p. 11); untested expert creativity means were 4.23 vs 4.35 in Study 1 and 4.86 vs 4.52 in Study 2 (Appendix D, p. 18).
open_questions: Study 2 exclusions and category coding: five ideas and three participants were excluded for unrelatedness (p. 9, Section 5.1), yet an out-of-instruction-scope category with five ideas remains in the coding scheme (p. 9, Section 5.4; Appendix C, p. 16); authors or the analysis data are needed to establish whether this category enters the main breadth scores.

Per-arm exclusions are not explicitly reported. Total exclusions and randomized and analyzed arm counts are confirmed in each study, but author confirmation would be needed to document the exclusion reasons and allocation by arm without inferring them.

Similarity analyses: the PDF does not state whether Table 7 SDs are computed over pairs or idea-level averages, or what denominator the reported similarity Cohen's d uses; obtain the analysis method or code before treating these as participant-level uncertainty for pooling.

Study 2 similarity: the first-idea selection rule is implied by the description of analyses parallel to Study 1 and the idea Ns in Table 7, but is not explicitly restated; the sign convention of M difference = 0.01 is also unstated while both arm means round to 0.87 (p. 10, Section 5.5.2; p. 11, Table 7).

Study 1 stimulus-pool comparison: the pool mean used for M difference = -0.10 is not printed (p. 8, Section 4.6.2). The earlier cleaned-pool similarity of 0.69 (p. 7, Section 4.2) cannot be substituted without confirming the same preprocessing and analysis.

Study 1 usefulness and creativity: Appendix D (p. 18) says a third usefulness item was dropped after Study 1, but does not establish whether the reported Study 1 scores include it; this is also the unresolved reconciliation difference for S1-O6.

Possible sample overlap: establish whether c117 Study 1 shares participants with c917, Sorin and Pagani (2022), Artificial Intelligence Systems: the Influence on Human Entrepreneurial Creativity, DOI 10.5465/ambpp.2022.12146abstract, or with their cited 2023 chapter When artificial intelligence systems help to inspire creative new venture ideas. The c917 local search/triage records describe a 90-participant venture-idea experiment, but that description is an unverified lead. The c117 acknowledgement of prior AOM presentations (p. 13) does not establish participant identity. OpenAlex W4286621575 and the Crossref DOI endpoint could not be accessed during finalization because both requests failed with WinError 10013; no confirmed shared sample is recorded.

Study 1 country is not stated. International student status and language choice do not establish recruitment country (p. 6, Section 4.1); online_rct is supported by the online individual procedure (p. 8, Section 4.5).

Idea length/elaboration: Appendix D (p. 19) states that AI-exposed participants produced shorter ideas on average, but identifies neither the study nor the length measure, aggregation unit, analyzed sample or statistics. Obtain author clarification before assigning this paper-level directional observation to a study-specific outcome; the finding is retained in notes.
notes: Both studies ran before ChatGPT's public release. The AI aid is a static list of pre-generated ideas, not interactive use, and both Study 1 arms were told they could do internet research (Appendix B, p. 14). The paper's two primary outcome tests are breadth (hypothesized) and depth (not hypothesized), Holm-Bonferroni corrected (p. 8, Section 4.6.1). It labels the similarity analyses and the expert ratings complementary or exploratory. Manipulation checks: 78 percent (Study 1) and 92 percent (Study 2) said they understood the ideas came from AI; dropping the others leaves results unchanged (p. 7; p. 9). Appendix D (p. 19, Interpretation) states that AI-exposed participants produced shorter ideas on average and interprets this as reduced elaboration. This is retained as a paper-level output observation: construct elaboration, question with_ai, direction treatment_lower, statistics_available [none]. The text presents it as a plausible explanation and supplies no length measure, analysis unit, study attribution or numerical results. No study-specific record is assigned until those missing details are clarified; the observation must not be duplicated across the two studies or used as an estimate. Section 5.5.3 (p. 11) also discusses more superficial ideas, without a length analysis. The paper calls the generator fine-tuned; Section 7 (p. 13) and Appendix A describe the domain examples and human feedback as given through prompting. Outcome ids follow screener A; screener B's S1-O4 and S2-O4 (stimulus-pool comparisons) are S1-O8 and S2-O8 here, and B's O5-O8 are O4-O7. Finalization also corrected the Study 1 control-interface locator to p. 7, Section 4.2, and removed unreported per-arm exclusion counts inferred by subtraction. Primary-record selection is settled by codebook Section 8: the paper-primary, hypothesized breadth outcome takes precedence over the secondary expert creativity rating; breadth is selected ahead of the unhypothesized depth check. The reconciliation object is preserved as the historical reconciliation, including its unresolved usefulness-item question.
